en: // Chapter on the Objects of Cognition //
// The Second Daily Lesson //

Nyāyapraveśaka, Prameya-section, 9: Here, although everything whose nature is non-superimposed is "knowable" (*prameya*) by virtue of the etymological derivation that "the knowable is the object of valid cognition" (*pramā-viṣaya*), intended for the purpose of excluding superimposed forms, nevertheless—because it is an internal factor for the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*)—that which is to be measured with excellence (*prakṛṣṭa-meya*) is what is intended here as "the knowable" (*prameya*).
It is that object concerning which we wander in saṃsāra due to delusion.
That object through the knowledge of whose reality we may attain liberation is here our primary object of cognition (*prameya*).

And that has been stated as being of twelve kinds by Akṣapāda: "The self, body, sense organs, objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation are the objects of cognition."
In that regard, the self is conscious;
it is of two kinds: the Lord (Īśvara) and the non-Lord (an-īśvara). The Lord is the creator of the world.
The Lord is devoid of worldly activity; He is consciousness.
That substance which has the same locus as His consciousness, which is not established separately from it, is His body.
That is of two kinds: born of action and not born of action;
the former belongs to those such as ourselves.
The second [view] is that of Īśvara and others:
the sense organ (*indriya*) is a substance whose material cause (*upādāna*) is the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*).
It is of eleven kinds: the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*), [the five organs of action, and the mind].
The five organs of action and the mind— these are the sense-faculties; the objects of these faculties are the "meanings" (artha) here,
namely sound and the other qualities, as well as those things characterized by them.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is the illumination of objects;
the mind (*manas*), as the instrument of memory and so forth, is the sense-organ (*indriya*);
and here, "activity" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the meritorious and non-meritorious operations of the mind, speech, and body.

The defects (*doṣa*) are the causes for such activity; and these, in brief, are attachment, aversion, and delusion. Rebirth (*pretyabhāva*) is the acquisition of a subsequent body after leaving a previous one.
The fruit is that which is to be accomplished through activity; that very thing, when intended by a person as the goal of activity, is the purpose (*prayojana*).
Pain (*duḥkha*) is that which is experienced as disagreeable.

In this regard, even pleasure and its means should be regarded as nothing but suffering by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), because they are accompanied by manifold evils, like honey mixed with poison; thus, they too are to be experienced as disagreeable.
Liberation (*apavarga*) is the cessation of suffering that does not coexist with the causes of other forms of suffering.

And that [cessation] consists in the experience of Brahman—which is characterized by unsurpassed bliss and all-pervading attributes—preceded by the manifestation of the soul’s own innate nature; it is therefore the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).
Or rather, liberation is preceded by that [knowledge] and culminates in such an experience of Brahman.

And it is precisely this object of knowledge (*prameya*) that some, having divided it into four categories for the sake of summary, connect as follows: "that which is to be abandoned (*heya*), that which brings about its cessation (*tannivartaka*)," and so forth.
Furthermore,
the means for that [liberation] is as follows:
whereas those such as Kaṇāda and Caraka examine all categories by dividing them into groups of six, seven, and so forth, [the Sāṃkhya method is different].
These [categories] have been refuted by rejecting the status of generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth as distinct categories (*padārtha*).
Consequently, only three remain: substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).

Even there, although action is accepted by some as being distinct from qualities, it is nonetheless subsumed under the category of quality—just like specific sub-types of quality such as *saṃskāra* (disposition)—and thus there are only two categories.

Furthermore, since the word "quality" (guṇa) is conventionally understood as a mere non-separately established attribute and yet applies to certain substances as well, it would be inappropriate to divide categories into the forms of "substance" and "quality"; therefore, we adopt the division of categories simply as "substance" and "non-substance.
Such an inquiry, however, is of use indirectly for the attainment of liberation (apavarga).

Considering that for those seeking liberation the most primary object of knowledge (*prameya*) is the one, distinguished Brahman alone, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa begins with the words, "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*), and treats that very [Brahman] as the object of knowledge along with its modes, while other things are objects of knowledge only by virtue of being such modes. However, some, following the sequence of discriminating the body from the self and in accordance with the method of the Śruti which says, "Having understood the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller," divide reality into three categories and reflect upon them accordingly.

In that regard as well, because the investigation of substances includes their various modes (*saprakāra*), the investigation of non-substances (*adravya*) is also included. By the same logic, the investigation of time (*kāla*) is likewise included.

With this intention, since time is subsumed within the cognition of all things precisely as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of entities, its existence and other such properties need not be stated separately.

Nor should they be avoided; for at the time of refuting the Jains, the Commentator stated: "The conventional usage among speakers regarding 'time exists' or 'time does not exist' is equivalent to the conventional usage regarding the existence or non-existence of birth and so forth. Furthermore, [the view that] Brahman alone is the single reality, or [the view] through the distinction of consciousness, unconscious matter, and the Lord—[these are to be understood as follows].

For those who view [reality] as consisting of three principles (*tattva*), there is no difference whatsoever, because both schools accept a distinction in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) as well as a specific unity (*viśiṣṭaikya*).
For this very reason: "Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), Spirit (*puruṣa*), the Manifest (*vyakta*), and Time (*kāla*), indeed, [are distinguished] by their respective divisions."
"Forms are the causes of stability, creation, dissolution, manifestation, and existence."

According to such passages, for those who contemplate by dividing [the principles] into four or five categories, and who assign numbers such as five, six, seven, or twenty-seven along with specific effects, no difference from the previous [view] is heard; and it is stated in scripture: "They call him the twenty-sixth, while others say the twenty-seventh;
the Atharvaśiras know the Puruṣa to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), according to Sāṃkhya."
Thus:
that which is to be attained, the attainment, and the means of attainment.

Some enumerate the objects of cognition (*prameya*) as fivefold: the means of knowledge, the object, doubt, purpose, and the result; others, including the specific relationship (*saṃbandha*), say there are six.
Nyāyabindu, Pramāṇapariccheda 10: Now, this other summary [of objects] for the sake of purposeful activity is internal to the process of engagement and avoidance;
for instance, the beneficial and the harmful are the objects to be measured with excellence.

In that regard, regarding worldly benefit and harm, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists of the science of medicine (*āyurveda*), the science of ethics (*nītiśāstra*), and so forth, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Even that [worldly conduct] must be followed by one seeking liberation for the sake of preserving the body, which serves as the instrument for the practice of yoga, provided it does not conflict with the Śruti, Smṛti, and other authorities.
Regarding the extraordinary (alaukika) beneficial and harmful, however, the Vedas are the authority;
and the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas serve to supplement them.
And whatever is prescribed by the Śruti, all that is beneficial according to one's qualification;
and whatever is prohibited therein—
All of that is indeed harmful.

Now, one might ask: how can rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), which are causes of misfortune, and those optional rites (*kāmya-karman*) intended for the attainment of inferior human goals (*puruṣārtha*), be considered beneficial?
It is said in reply: for every injunction and prohibition is indeed relative to a specific qualified person (*adhikārin*).
As it has been said: "The Vedas have the three *guṇas* as their subject matter.

For one who desires pleasure and the cessation of suffering, and who, seeking the means thereto, engages in worldly means, those [worldly means] are found to be causes of harm by being the causes of states such as hell; therefore, for the sake of avoiding them, [one seeks] those [means] that are free from being causes of harm.
The means for attaining happiness and so forth are being set forth.

In this way, rites performed out of desire for the sake of the next world—which have results either similar to those seen in this life or superior to them—are indeed beneficial for those possessed of passion, because they serve as a means to obstruct engagement in pleasures that bring about visible harm.
The same applies to rites pertaining to this world, such as the Citra sacrifice and others.

However, rites such as the Kārīrī, though beneficial to the world, do not constitute a cause of harm by their very nature, even though they include malevolent magic (abhicāra) involving acts of violence and the like; for the animal slaughter that is a subordinate part (aṅga) of those rites is sanctioned by injunction, just like the sacrifice to Agni and Soma.
Rather, it is with respect to the killing of a victim who has not yet reached the state of being one's own object of accomplishment that malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is prohibited;
for even that [magic] must indeed be performed in certain circumstances.

Because of such scriptural indications as, "One falls [from his status] by practicing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) against the six [classes of persons]," even for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), malevolent magic must indeed be performed for the sake of self-protection in the absence of a protecting Kṣatriya or similar protector, or when one is overwhelmed by Rākṣasas and the like;
for there is the scriptural injunction: "One should protect oneself from all [hazards]."

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the interruption of rites and other practices that must be performed day by day and continued until death; this would result in the failure to accomplish the means [to liberation] and thus the impossibility of attaining mokṣa.

Furthermore, all meditations (upāsanā) having visible purposes, such as rain and food, must be performed whenever they are required, as they serve as the means for accomplishing those specific meditations.

Those [rites] pertaining to the next world, however, should be performed during the stage of practicing Karma-yoga without any desire for their fruits, by integrating them with the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites.

For all occasional rites (*naimittika*) are indeed beneficial to all, as they serve to avoid the undesirable consequences that have arisen; likewise are the obligatory rites (*nitya*), because they serve to qualify one for subsequent rituals and to avoid the transgression caused by their non-performance.
Therefore, everything prescribed by the Śruti and appropriate to one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) is indeed beneficial.
For this very reason, they record in the Smṛti: "The scripture is indeed more affectionate than a thousand mothers and fathers.

This being the case, through the power of the beginningless cycle of causal conditions (*sāmagrīcakra*), there arises that which is well-protected by all established philosophical systems (*siddhāntika*) when they assemble at an indefinite time.

By the power of his own being, which has been awakened by the special glance of the Supreme Person—whose obstacles to the ripening of others have ceased—one perceives, as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of the hand, the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; one becomes detached from the honey of worldly pleasures, which are full of meager and unstable joys defiled by the attachment to manifold, unbearable, and beginningless and endless sufferings;
and one becomes intent upon the nectar of service to the lotus feet of Mukunda, which brings about the removal of the entire mass of evils and consists of eternal, unsurpassed bliss.

The worship of the Blessed Lord— which consists of constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) whose form is identical to direct perception, and which is accompanied by the performance of obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and prohibited-avoidance (*niṣiddhaparihāra*) duties as appropriate to one's caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*) according to one's capacity—

is ordained as the most beneficial. This worship is manifold, being divided into the *sad-akṣara-nyāsa*, *vaiśvānara*, *madhu*, *bhūma*, *dahara*, and other types, and it is to be accomplished by all three castes and all stages of life.
And because it consists of unsurpassed love for the supremely venerable object, it is denoted by the word *bhakti*.
This alone is the supreme yoga propounded in all the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) that follow the Upanishads;
as the blessed Parāśara said: "That particular movement of the mind which depends upon personal effort..."
The union with that Brahman is designated as Yoga.”
Thus it is said;
and the Blessed Śāṇḍilya records: "This Supreme Self is such, and the inner self (pratyagātman) is likewise such;
the contemplation of their relationship is proclaimed as Yoga."
Thus,
in this regard, Sāṃkhya is helpful for the mere discernment between the conscious and the unconscious,
while Yoga is helpful for purifying the equipment for samādhi, such as the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama).
Regarding specific duties, the Karmakāṇḍa and other such texts are authoritative;
the Pañcarātra is authoritative everywhere.
As for the categories of prohibited and optional acts, as well as those that are futile or not mandatory, [the Pañcarātra is authoritative].
The injunction for tranquility and so forth is not contradicted by engagement in other matters.
This very dharma, known as the supreme yoga, is proclaimed thus: "Fix your mind on Me alone.
For one who is unable to do that:
"But if you are not able to fix the mind steadily on Me..."
"O Dhanañjaya, he who has reached Me through the yoga of practice desires to attain Me;
if you are unable to practice, then become intent upon My work."
By these and other such statements, the preceding stages are prescribed.

For one who is not even capable of performing the unique deeds of the Blessed One out of love, [the following is taught] in order to produce an aversion toward the taste of sense-objects, even for that which has been contemplated for a very long time as the remainder of all worldly pleasures.

To behold the nature of one's own self as an bliss exceeding all worldly pleasures, there are two medicines for tearing away the veil of cataracts that obstruct the inner eye: those known as the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) and the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
Among these, the yoga of knowledge, consisting of reflection upon the Self, is the internal means for that vision.
Even in that case, for one who is incapable, there is the yoga of action (karmayoga) for the sake of establishing eligibility for that [higher path].
Therefore, even for one whose eligibility is established therein and who is designated as a refined person (śiṣṭa), since self-knowledge is internalized, the yoga of action alone must be performed.

Otherwise, even for this person who knows the whole, the yoga of knowledge would be obstructed by the power of a greater evil—the root of which is the generation of a distinction in the intellect of a person who knows only a part—due to his incapacity for the yoga of knowledge despite knowing the whole.

And by means of such *karmayoga* itself—which possesses qualities such as ease of practice and so forth—if it is performed for a long time, the vision of the Self is accomplished even without the intervention of *jñānayoga*.
However, one who is incapable even of *karmayoga* should nevertheless undertake it, however incomplete it may be; for, "In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor is any obstacle found."
"Even a very small amount of this Dharma protects one from great fear."
Because it is established through such passages that even when deficiencies or interruptions occur, there is an invariable concomitance with the fruit;
thus, the Blessed One, being pleased by the mere commencement [of the rite], brings about its completeness.

Furthermore, in all these festivals, for the sake of assembling the respective circles of causal conditions (*sāmagrīcakra*) and for the bestowal of their respective fruits, he alone is indeed the refuge to be sought.
And thus they declare: "That is the limit, that is the supreme goal.
The meaning is that this very Supreme Person is the ultimate state of mastery and the supreme object of attainment.
Regarding this, the Commentary states: "And his mastery consists precisely in taking refuge in him."
Thus, a mere indication of the direction regarding this most beneficial form of worship has been shown;
and its fruit, which consists of liberation (apavarga), has already been characterized.

For others, however, [liberation] consists of the mere severance of the body; the cessation of the continuum of consciousness regarding all false objects such as the enjoyment of thousands of young women; the absolute cessation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); freedom from the coloring of sense-objects; eternal upward movement; entry into a particular common body situated above the summit of all worlds; unobstructedness; the attainment of sovereignty through the experience of one's own bliss; the state of being of the same form as Śiva (*śivasārūpya*), the attainment of Śiva (*śivāpatti*), the remaining of pure consciousness-power (*cicchakti*), the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), the removal of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and the destruction of all specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*), and so forth.

The various conceptions regarding the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)— such as the existence of a self distinct from the body and so forth, the ultimate reality of external objects, the invalidity of various scriptures, the changelessness and faultlessness of Brahman, and the eternity of its knowledge and bliss— are to be refuted by the treatises culminating in the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras), which establish these points. Thus, the details should be sought in the respective sections of those works.

However, in this context, the summary statement of the objects of cognition (prameya) is intended to demonstrate the ultimate purpose of the investigation into the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), since the treatise on the expansion of reasoning (nyāyavistara-śāstra) is devoted to establishing the boundaries of the means of valid cognition along with their auxiliary factors.

Where Jaimini and others, intent on contemplating the meaning of the Vedas, remained indifferent; and where those of dull intellect produce only wavering and confused arguments—here, for the repose of all disputants, the ancient path through the Nīti texts has been thoroughly cleared by the scholar Veṅkaṭeśa, providing abundant shade and free from thorns.

The utterances of those like me possess purity solely within the lineage of the Cūḍā; only at the end was something mixed spoken by those skilled in policy—is there any need for it to be considered authoritative among them?

Having reflected upon the sequence of the *saradhā* and *puṣpa* in the pair of sections, my composition—a collection of virtues whose excellence cannot be denied—should be accepted by those who reason.
When the three Vedas have become firmly established, which are the wish-fulfilling gems for all the world and the locus for the devotion of those who offer prayers;
when one takes delight in that Brahman, whose nature is shared by Lakṣmī, the Earth, and Dharma, then meditative cultivation quickly reaches a state of dissolution.

Thus ends the second Āhnika in the Prameya-adhyāya of the Nyāyapariśuddhi, among the works of the venerable Vedāntācārya Śrīmad Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians, who is independent in all systems of thought;
and thus the fifth Adhyāya is completed.
And the treatise is completed.
Salutations to the venerable Nigamānta Mahādeśika.
